label: lem:reduction
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: reduction

title: Proof
body_md: Maximizing $\operatorname{Re}(e^{\mathrm i\theta}z_\sigma)$ over $\theta$ in~\eqref{eq:rotation-cost} gives $|z_\sigma|$. The modulus is convex, so its maximum over the polygon is attained at a vertex, and every vertex is the correlation of a matching. \Cref{app:reduction} treats reflections and zero correlations.

name: Proof sketch

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For every $n\ge2$ and all $a,b\in\mathbb C^n$, the polygon $\mathcal{P}(a,b)$ has at most $n(n-1)$ vertices. Consequently, for any two equally weighted planar sets of $n$ points there are at most $n(n-1)$ matchings such that, for every rotation, one of them is optimal. For generic point sets, that is, when $(\bar x,y)$ is generic in the sense of \Cref{def:generic}, the optimal matching is unique for all but finitely many angles and changes at most $n(n-1)$ times over a full turn. The bound is attained for every $n$ (\Cref{prop:tight}).
head: environment

label: lem:cycle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cycle}
For generic $(a,b)$ and $u\in\mathbb C$ with $|u|=1$, maximizing $\operatorname{Re}(\bar uz_\sigma)$ gives either a unique permutation or two permutations $\sigma,\tau$ for which $\sigma^{-1}\tau$ is a single nontrivial cycle.
head: environment
name: cycle transitions

title: Proof
body_md: Under genericity, a supporting line contains at most two correlations, so at most two matchings are optimal in any direction. If two are optimal, switching any single cycle of their difference leaves the projection unchanged: the cycles act on disjoint rows, so their changes of the projection add up to zero, and none of them is positive. Two nontrivial cycles would therefore produce a third optimal matching, a contradiction. The full proof is in \Cref{app:cycle-transitions}.
head: environment
name: Proof sketch

label: lem:jump
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: jump

title: Proof
body_md: For $L_e\ge3$, we move each reassigned point linearly from its old position to its new one along the corresponding edge of $\Gamma_e$. The power-diagram construction makes $\Gamma_e$ simple and counterclockwise, with no off-cycle point on its boundary. The moving points do not collide, because they follow distinct edges of the polygon and reach shared endpoints at different times. Optimality at both ends of the motion keeps every swap gain, multiplied by $\bar u$, in the closed right half-plane, so the contribution of each pair to the phase jump equals the continuous change of its argument. To evaluate these changes, we deform $\Gamma_e$ continuously into a regular polygon, which shows that the pairs of moving points contribute $\pi(L_e-1)$ in total. Each off-cycle point enclosed by $\Gamma_e$ contributes a further $2\pi$, and each off-cycle point outside contributes zero. For $L_e=2$, the swapped pair contributes $\pi$ directly, and its contributions relative to each off-cycle point cancel. Adding these terms gives~\eqref{eq:jump}. The full proof, including the orientation of the cycle and the two-point case, is in \Cref{app:jump}.
head: environment
name: Proof sketch

label: lem:counting
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: counting identity

title: Proof
body_md: The continuous decrease of the phase~\eqref{eq:phase} over a full turn is $\pi n(n-1)$, and the jumps must restore it. Substituting~\eqref{eq:jump} for each jump and dividing by $\pi$ gives the identity. \Cref{fig:phase} illustrates the case $n=7$; \Cref{app:phase-total,app:counting-bound} give the full accounting.
head: environment

label: lem:semicont
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:semicont}
For every $(a,b)$ and $\delta_{\mathrm{pert}}>0$ there is a generic $(a',b')$ within distance $\delta_{\mathrm{pert}}$ with $\#\mathrm{vert}\,\mathcal{P}(a',b')\ge\#\mathrm{vert}\,\mathcal{P}(a,b)$.
head: environment
name: semicontinuity

title: Proof
body_md: For each vertex of the original polygon we choose a direction that exposes it strictly. The score gaps in these finitely many directions are positive and persist under sufficiently small perturbations, so each of the disjoint neighborhoods of the original vertices contains an extreme point of the perturbed polygon. Generic pairs are dense by \Cref{lem:generic}, so the perturbation can be chosen generic. The full proof is in \Cref{app:semicontinuity}.
head: environment
name: Proof sketch

title: Proof
body_md: For generic inputs with $n\ge3$, every summand in \Cref{lem:counting} is at least one, so the polygon has at most $n(n-1)$ edges and hence at most $n(n-1)$ vertices. For arbitrary inputs, a polygon that is a single point satisfies the bound directly; otherwise \Cref{lem:semicont} gives a nearby generic polygon with at least as many vertices, which extends the bound to every input. For $n=2$ there are only two permutations. The statement about matchings holds because one representative matching per vertex contains an optimal matching for every direction (\Cref{sec:correlations}), and under genericity only the two adjacent vertices tie at an edge normal. \Cref{prop:tight} proves sharpness. The complete arguments for the bound and for sharpness are in \Cref{app:counting-bound,app:tightness}, respectively.

label: prop:tight
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:tight}
For $n\ge2$, if $a\in\mathbb R^n$ has distinct entries and $b\in\mathbb C^n$ has distinct entries with pairwise non-parallel differences $b_j-b_l$, $j<l$, then $\mathcal{P}(a,b)$ has exactly $n(n-1)$ vertices.

label: cor:weights
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:weights}
Let $\mu_X=\sum_i\alpha_i\delta_{x_i}$ and $\mu_Y=\sum_j\beta_j\delta_{y_j}$ with nonnegative rational weights summing to one and common denominator $N\ge1$, where $\delta_x$ denotes a unit point mass at $x$. Remove zero-weight atoms, and let $\Pi(\alpha,\beta)$ be the nonnegative matrices with row sums $\alpha$ and column sums $\beta$. Then $\{\sum_{ij}\pi_{ij}\bar x_iy_j:\pi\in\Pi(\alpha,\beta)\}$ has at most $\max\{1,N(N-1)\}$ vertices. In particular, for uniform weights on $n$ and $m$ points, it has at most $\max\{1,N_{\mathrm{uni}}(N_{\mathrm{uni}}-1)\}$ with $N_{\mathrm{uni}}=\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)$.
head: environment
name: rational weights

title: Proof
body_md: Replace each atom by as many copies of mass $1/N$ as the integer numerator of its weight. Aggregating the doubly stochastic matrices over these copies gives exactly the original transport polytope, so the weighted correlation polygon is a scaled equal-weight polygon. \Cref{thm:main} applies to it because repeated points are permitted; $N=1$ gives a single point. The full proof that replication preserves the set of feasible correlations is in \Cref{app:weights}.

name: Proof sketch

label: prop:es
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:es}
For $n\ge2$, \Cref{alg:rubix} returns the vertices of $\mathcal{P}$ using exactly $2V\le2n(n-1)$ calls to this oracle.
head: environment
name: polygon reconstruction

title: Proof
body_md: The two initial arcs are explored as two binary trees whose internal nodes are the splits and whose leaves are the confirmed edges. Together the trees have $V-2$ internal nodes and $V$ leaves, which with the two initial queries gives $2+(V-2)+V=2V$ calls. A single point needs two calls and a segment four, and the lexicographic tie-breaking keeps the returned points extreme for degenerate inputs. \Cref{app:reconstruction} proves the invariant and the count.

name: Proof sketch

label: cor:pw
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:pw}
For $n\ge2$, Rubix computes planar $\mathrm{PW}$ exactly with at most $2n(n-1)$ lexicographic assignment problems (oracle calls) over $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ and $4n(n-1)$ over $\mathrm{O}(2)$, and $\mathcal{O}(n^5)$ arithmetic operations. For $n=1$ the solution is immediate.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Apply \Cref{prop:es} to $\mathcal{P}(\bar x,y)$ and, over $\mathrm{O}(2)$, to $\mathcal{P}(\bar x,\bar y)$, then use \Cref{lem:reduction}. Each call costs $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ operations; see \Cref{app:pw-complexity}.

name: Proof sketch

label: prop:optimality
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:optimality}
Let $a,b$ have rational real and imaginary parts, and let $\widehat{\mathcal P}$ be the hull of the correlations recomputed from the returned matchings, with its distinct extreme points and their boundary order verified exactly. Suppose that assignment duals certify the following support values. If $\widehat{\mathcal P}$ is two-dimensional, they certify its support value in the outward normal direction of every edge. If it is a segment, they certify its line through the two opposite normal directions and its endpoints through the two extrema along the line. If it is a single point, they certify that the two opposite primary extrema coincide and that the two opposite secondary extrema coincide. Then $\widehat{\mathcal P}=\mathcal P(a,b)$, and comparing the squared moduli of its vertices gives $\max_{z\in\mathcal P(a,b)}|z|^2$ exactly.
head: environment
name: Exact global verification

title: Proof
body_md: Every point used to form $\widehat{\mathcal P}$ is the correlation of a matching, so $\widehat{\mathcal P}\subseteq\mathcal P$. The verified supporting half-planes contain $\mathcal P$ and intersect in $\widehat{\mathcal P}$, which gives the reverse inclusion. The checks for a segment and for a single point establish the same inclusion in lower dimension. By convexity, a farthest point is a vertex. The full proof is in \Cref{app:verification}.
head: environment
name: Proof sketch

label: prop:am
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:am}
For $\mathrm{SO}(2)$, the correlation moduli produced by AM~\cite{adamo2025} never decrease. Suppose that AM is initialized by an assignment step and that each assignment step returns a vertex and keeps the current matching when it is optimal. Then every matching that AM visits has a vertex correlation, and such a matching with nonzero correlation is a fixed point exactly when its vertex is stationary. Starting from a nonzero vertex correlation, these updates reach a fixed matching after at most $V-1$ matching changes, with $V-1\le n(n-1)-1$ for $n\ge2$. A farthest vertex is globally optimal. At zero correlation, any rotation is a valid update, and if $\mathcal{P}=\{0\}$, all rotations are globally optimal.
head: environment
name: finite convergence and fixed points of AM

title: Proof
body_md: For $z\ne0$, set $u=z/|z|$ and let $z'$ be the next correlation. Then $|z'|\ge\operatorname{Re}(\bar uz')\ge\operatorname{Re}(\bar uz)=|z|$, and under the retention rule the second inequality is strict whenever the matching changes. Each change therefore reaches a vertex that has not been visited before, which allows at most $V-1$ changes. A matching is retained exactly when its correlation is optimal in its own radial direction, which is the stationarity of its vertex. \Cref{app:am} treats ties and zero correlations.

name: Proof sketch

label: prop:gravity-accuracy
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:gravity-accuracy}
For complete matching after centering, or partial matching at a supplied
translation, put $\boldsymbol w_M=(\alpha_M,\beta_M)$ and $\kappa_\theta=2\max_M\|\boldsymbol w_M\|$.
Without an external budget, \Cref{alg:gravity-yaw}, initialized by three equal
arcs, reaches summed-objective gap $\varepsilon>0$ with
$\mathcal O(1+\sqrt{\kappa_\theta/\varepsilon})$ assignment queries.
head: environment
name: Conditional-yaw accuracy

title: Proof
body_md: Moving the tangent apex to the midpoint of the arc on the circle changes the cost of a matching by at most $\kappa_\theta(\sec h_\theta-1)\le\kappa_\theta h_\theta^2$ for $h_\theta\le\pi/3$. Bisection therefore reaches the required local gap within $\mathcal O(1+\sqrt{\kappa_\theta/\varepsilon})$ cells. If $\kappa_\theta=0$, the objective is constant in the yaw. \Cref{app:gravity-accuracy} proves the gap and the query count.

name: Proof sketch

label: prop:bound-order
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bound-order}
Fix the translation, or eliminate it by centering. Let $A$ be a yaw arc of
half-width $h_\theta\in(0,\pi/3]$, let $F^*_A=\min_{\theta\in A}F(u(\theta))$, and let $L_A$ denote the lower bound on $A$ under consideration.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item The Rubix interpolant bound satisfies $F^*_A-L_A\le \kappa_\theta h_\theta^2$, with $\kappa_\theta$ as in
\Cref{prop:gravity-accuracy}, and $F^*_A=L_A$ whenever one matching attains all
three triangle values.
\item The per-correspondence radius bound of Yang et al.~\cite{yang2016goicp}, specialized to yaw,
\[
\min_M\sum_{(i,j)\in M}(\|R_\mu x_i-y_j\|-2\sin(h_\theta/2)\|x_{i,xy}\|)_+^2
\]
and the independent-edge bound
\[
\min_M\sum_{(i,j)\in M}\min_{\theta\in A}\|R_\theta x_i-y_j\|^2
\]
are first order: there are instances with $F^*_A-L_A\ge c h_\theta$ on the arcs
centered at the minimizer, for a constant $c>0$ independent of $h_\theta$.
\item On the radius-bound instance of~(ii), best-first bisection using that bound,
a zero floor, and inherited maxima expands $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$ arcs to
certify an absolute gap $\varepsilon<1$, while the Rubix bound certifies the
optimum after evaluating the three root arcs. This comparison excludes
additional global bounds.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Second-order coupled bounds

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) is the local gap in the proof of \Cref{prop:gravity-accuracy}; a common
supporting matching makes the interpolant exact by \Cref{lem:arc-interpolation}.
For~(ii), note that the two displayed comparison bounds rotate the source set. One source point $(1,0,0)$ and one target $(2,0,0)$ give
$F=5-4\cos\theta$ and a radius-bound gap of $4\sin(h_\theta/2)-4\sin^2(h_\theta/2)\ge2h_\theta/\pi$; two
points whose edges prefer the yaws $\pm a$, with $\pi/3\le a<\pi/2$, give an independent-edge gap of
$8\sin(a-h_\theta/2)\sin(h_\theta/2)\ge(8/\pi)\sin(a/2)\,h_\theta$. For~(iii), we credit each inherited bound to the ancestor
at which it was evaluated and contract its descendant subtree there. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, every terminal
descendant of the central root that meets
$[-\sqrt\varepsilon,\sqrt\varepsilon]$ has half-width below $100\varepsilon$.
Covering this interval therefore requires at least $1/(100\sqrt\varepsilon)$ leaves
and $1/(200\sqrt\varepsilon)$ expansions. The objective for a single correspondence is
affine in the lifted yaw coordinates, so the Rubix bound is exact on all three
root arcs. The full proof and the first-order constructions are in \Cref{app:bound-order}.

label: rem:unbalanced
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:unbalanced}
The penalty on unmatched points has a transport interpretation. Give every point unit mass. At a fixed pose, unbalanced transport with a total-variation penalty on the marginals minimizes $\sum_{ij}P_{ij}c_{ij}+\lambda(\|\mathbf 1-P\mathbf 1\|_1+\|\mathbf 1-P^\top\mathbf 1\|_1)$ over nonnegative $P$, where $c_{ij}=\|x_i-Ry_j-t\|^2$. Reducing the excess mass in a row decreases the penalty of that row by at least as much as it increases the penalties of the columns, and it does not increase the transport cost. The same argument applies to columns, so some optimal $P$ satisfies $P\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$ and $P^\top\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$. The objective is then $\sum_{ij}P_{ij}(c_{ij}-2\lambda)+\lambda(n+m)$, which is linear on the bipartite matching polytope, whose vertices are the partial matchings. The penalized objective~\eqref{eq:partial-spatial} is therefore rigid unbalanced transport with this penalty. With zero heights, \Cref{alg:gravity-yaw} computes it over planar rotations at a supplied translation and reaches a gap of $\varepsilon$ with $\mathcal O(1+\sqrt{\kappa_\theta/\varepsilon})$ assignment queries, because its arc bounds are second order (\Cref{prop:gravity-accuracy,prop:bound-order}). Unbalanced GW~\cite{sejourne2021} instead compares the internal distances of the two sets under marginals relaxed by a Kullback--Leibler penalty and is solved by local alternation; \Cref{sec:exp-unbalanced} compares the two.

label: lem:joint-cover
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:joint-cover}
For prescribed cardinality $k>0$ and a feasible cost $U$, the $nm$ forced-anchor
domains above, with radius $\sqrt{U/k}$, cover every
improving pose and matching. For penalties, the same holds after partitioning
by $k$, subtracting $p_k=\lambda(n+m-2k)$ from $U$, retaining all branches
with $p_k\le U$, and testing the empty matching separately. Within one branch,
let $W$ be any feasible matching of size $k$. On every yaw-triangle/translation-box
cell, the slack in \eqref{eq:gravity-joint-slack} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-witness-guarantee}
 \min_M E_M(\theta,e)\ge E_W(\theta,e)-\Delta_W.
\end{equation}
If $W$ supports all 24 product vertices, equality holds throughout the cell.

title: Proof

Every selection has $k$ pairs and hence the same quadratic term in the translation, so $F_{\rm red}=F-k\|t-c_B\|^2$ is concave in $u$ and concave in $t$ separately. label: thm:spatial-covariance
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:spatial-covariance}
For equally weighted complete point sets of the same positive size in
$\mathbb R^3$, the optimal proper rigid residual is \eqref{eq:se3-polytope}.
Some vertex of $\mathcal C$ attains its maximum, and any unit top eigenvector
of its quaternion matrix gives an optimal rotation; translation is
$m_x-Rm_y$. If the centered point sets have ranks $r_X,r_Y$, then
$\dim\mathcal C=r_Xr_Y\le9$. Repeated points, rank deficiency, and eigenvalue
ties are allowed. Rational inputs admit a finite exact polytope reduction,
without a claimed polynomial vertex or facet count.

title: Proof
body_md: Write $\tilde q=\sum_a\alpha_a\tilde q_a$ with convex weights. Expanding the normalized lift gives a convex combination of the corner and cross-corner lifts, because their dot products are positive. Convexity of $H$, which is a maximum of linear functions, gives the first bound. Subtracting the linear score of the witness before interpolating, and then applying the Rayleigh inequality, gives the second. \Cref{app:quaternion-lifts,app:quaternion-cover} prove the enclosure, the coverage by charts and the convergence under refinement.

label: prop:partial-moments
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:partial-moments}
For finite point sets and either prescribed cardinality
$0\le k\le\min(n,m)$ or a positive unmatched penalty, freely translated partial
proper-rigid alignment attains an optimum at
a vertex of the convex hull of matching statistics
\begin{equation}\label{eq:partial-moment-statistics}
 \Bigl(|M|,\sum_Mx_i,\sum_My_j,\sum_M(\|x_i\|^2+\|y_j\|^2),\sum_Mx_i y_j^\top\Bigr).
\end{equation}
The vector coordinates $\boldsymbol s_{X,M}=\sum_Mx_i$ and $\boldsymbol s_{Y,M}=\sum_My_j$ are coordinate sums, not centroids; write $S_M=\sum_M(\|x_i\|^2+\|y_j\|^2)$ and $C_M=\sum_Mx_i y_j^\top$ for the scalar norm sum and matrix correlation. This hull has dimension at most 17 and a linear support oracle given by partial
assignment. A nonempty vertex matching is evaluated by subset centering and
proper Procrustes alignment~\cite{horn1987}; the empty matching is evaluated separately.

name: Finite moment reduction for partial rigid alignment

title: Proof

label: thm:spatial-search
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:spatial-search}
Suppose the root domains cover every solution improving the initial feasible
incumbent, and every root is retained until validly pruned. Give each live region
$\Omega$ a valid residual lower bound
$L_\Omega$, replace it only by a complete finite child cover, and discard it
only when $L_\Omega\ge U$. Then every interruption preserves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:anytime-interval}
 \min\{U,\min_{\Omega\text{ live}}L_\Omega\}\le E^*\le U,
\end{equation}
with the empty minimum interpreted as $+\infty$. Without an external budget,
the specified conditional-yaw, joint-gravity, and quaternion searches terminate
at every $\varepsilon>0$, provided tightening eventually yields to subdivision
and every active coordinate shrinks along refined paths.
head: environment
name: Anytime interval and positive-tolerance termination

title: Proof
body_md: Feasible updates only decrease $U$, so pruned regions remain excluded; complete child covers and inherited bounds retain every other candidate. On the finite compact root cover, the bounds converge to the physical values as the cells shrink. An infinite refinement would contain an infinite path along which the gap tends to zero, which contradicts the stopping rule for a least-bound cell. \Cref{app:search-invariants} proves this argument, using the local convergence results of \Cref{app:gravity-accuracy,app:joint-convergence,app:quaternion-cover}; \Cref{app:spatial-queue} handles interruptions.

name: Proof sketch

title: Proof
body_md: For a fixed matching, minimizing \eqref{eq:rotation-cost} over the rotation replaces $\operatorname{Re}(e^{\mathrm i\theta}z_\sigma)$ by $|z_\sigma|$. The maximum of this convex function over the hull of the finitely many correlations is attained at a vertex, and every vertex is the correlation of a matching. For a nonzero maximum, $e^{\mathrm i\theta}z_\sigma=|z_\sigma|$ gives $\theta=-\operatorname{Arg} z_\sigma$; a zero maximum makes every rotation optimal. A reflection followed by a rotation replaces $y$ by $\bar y$, so comparing the two polygons covers $\mathrm O(2)$. The argument permits several optimal matchings and rotations.

label: def:generic
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:generic}
The pair $(a,b)$ is \emph{generic} if (G1) the map $\sigma\mapsto z_\sigma$ is injective and (G2) no three distinct points $z_\sigma$ are collinear.
head: environment

label: lem:generic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:generic}
The non-generic pairs are contained in a proper real-algebraic subset of $\mathbb C^{2n}\cong\mathbb R^{4n}$. In particular, generic pairs are dense and have full Lebesgue measure.

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $v_1,\dots,v_k$ be the vertices of $\mathcal P(a,b)$. For $k=1$ the claim holds because every polygon has at least one vertex. Otherwise, for each $v_l$ we choose a unit direction $u_l$ that exposes $v_l$ alone, and we choose $\delta>0$ below every positive score gap between $v_l$ and another correlation in direction $u_l$, and below half of every distance between two distinct vertices. By \Cref{lem:generic}, there is a generic pair within distance $\delta_{\mathrm{pert}}$ that moves each correlation by less than $\delta/3$. Every maximizer in direction $u_l$ then comes from a correlation that originally equaled $v_l$, so a vertex of the exposed face lies within $\delta/3$ of $v_l$, also when the face is an edge. These neighborhoods are disjoint, which yields at least $k$ distinct vertices.

title: Proof
body_md: By (G2), a supporting line contains at most two distinct correlations, and by (G1) these belong to at most two maximizing permutations. If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ both maximize, we decompose $\sigma^{-1}\tau$ into disjoint nontrivial cycles. Switching one cycle cannot raise the projection $\operatorname{Re}(\bar uz)$, because $\sigma$ is optimal. The cycles move disjoint rows, so these changes sum to the change from $\sigma$ to $\tau$, which is zero, and each of them is zero. If there were two cycles, switching only one of them would give a third maximizer, which contradicts genericity. Thus the relative permutation is a single nontrivial cycle.

label: lem:orient
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orient}
In the situation of Step~2 with $L\ge3$, $\chi_\Gamma>0$ if $\Gamma$ is counterclockwise and $\chi_\Gamma<0$ if it is clockwise. Hence $\Gamma$ is counterclockwise.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The region $D$ bounded by $\Gamma$ is a union of faces $Q$ of the subdivision, each dual to a vertex $v_Q$ of the diagram at which all sites of $Q$ are maximizers. We relate the orientation of each edge of the subdivision to that of its dual edge, and then sum over the enclosed faces to compare the contributions of the interior edges and of the boundary.

(i) \emph{Reciprocity.} Orient $e=y_l-y_j$ with $Q$ on its left. Its dual edge leaves $v_Q$ in the direction $R_-(e)$: the two tied scores keep $\langle\xi,e\rangle$ constant, while every other site of $Q$ loses maximality because $\langle R_-(e),y_k-y_j\rangle=-e\times(y_k-y_j)<0$. The opposite direction fails this inequality. If $Q'$ lies on the right of $e$, then $v_{Q'}=v_Q+\eta_e R_-(e)$ for some $\eta_e\ge0$.

(ii) \emph{Cancellation across faces.} For counterclockwise $\Gamma$, sum $\sum_{e\in\partial Q}v_Q\times e=0$ over the faces in $D$, with each boundary traversed counterclockwise. An interior edge contributes $(v_Q-v_{Q'})\times e=-\eta_e|e|^2$. Thus the outer boundary satisfies $\sum_rv_{Q_r}\times e_r=\sum_{\text{interior }e}\eta_e|e|^2\ge0$, where $Q_r$ lies to the left of $e_r$.

(iii) \emph{Strict positivity.} By (i), the point $\xi_{i_r}^{\mathrm{row}}$, which lies in the relative interior of the diagram edge dual to $e_r$, equals $v_{Q_r}+\eta_rR_-(e_r)$ with $\eta_r>0$. Therefore $\chi_\Gamma=\sum_rv_{Q_r}\times e_r+\sum_r\eta_r|e_r|^2>0$.
For clockwise $\Gamma$, reversing its edges to $-e_r$ gives $-\chi_\Gamma>0$ by the same computation.

label: lem:braid
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:braid}
Let $\Gamma=(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_L)$, $L\ge3$, be a simple polygon with indices modulo $L$, and let every vertex slide linearly to the next one, $\gamma_r(\zeta)=(1-\zeta)\gamma_r+\zeta\gamma_{r+1}$ for $0\le \zeta\le1$. Then $\Theta(\Gamma)=\pi(L-1)$ if $\Gamma$ is counterclockwise and $-\pi(L-1)$ if clockwise.

title: Proof
body_md: For generic inputs with $n\ge3$, substituting~\eqref{eq:jump} into \Cref{prop:total} and dividing by $\pi$ gives~\eqref{eq:counting}. Each term is at least one, so $V\le n(n-1)$. \Cref{lem:semicont} extends the bound to all inputs, and for $n=2$ there are at most two correlations. One representative matching per vertex covers all directions. Under genericity, the maximizing matching is unique between edge normals and changes once at each normal.

title: Proof
body_md:
We relabel so that $a_1<\cdots<a_n$. Abel's identity \eqref{eq:abel-summation} expresses each correlation through the positive increments $a_k-a_{k-1}$ and nested column sums. In a direction $u$, assigning the largest row weights to the largest projections $\operatorname{Re}(\bar u b_j)$ maximizes every sum simultaneously. Equality of the support functions shows that $\mathcal P$ is a translate of the Minkowski sum of positive multiples of $Q_h=\operatorname{conv}\{\sum_{j\in S}b_j:|S|=h\}$, $1\le h<n$.
It remains to count the changes in the order of the projections. For $n\ge3$, each pair exchanges its order twice, at the directions with $\operatorname{Re}(\bar u(b_j-b_l))=0$. Because the differences are non-parallel, all $2\binom n2$ transition directions are distinct. The tied columns are adjacent in the sorted order, so exactly one maximizing top-$h$ subset changes, which exposes one nondegenerate edge of one $Q_h$. Every other summand has a unique supporting vertex. The positive coefficient preserves this edge in the Minkowski sum, and no further transitions occur. Thus the polygon has exactly $n(n-1)$ edges and vertices. For $n=2$, the correlations differ by $(a_1-a_2)(b_1-b_2)\ne0$, which gives a segment with two vertices.

title: Proof
body_md: If the two initial outputs have the same correlation, both the real extrema and the opposite secondary imaginary extrema coincide. Thus $\mathcal P$ is a point and two calls suffice. Otherwise, the two initial chords represent complementary boundary arcs. A positive support gap splits its arc at a vertex strictly between the endpoints, and a zero gap confirms an edge. Pending arcs have disjoint interiors and exclude their endpoints, so no vertex is discovered twice: each query adds a vertex or confirms an edge. Each initial arc generates a binary tree with the splits as internal nodes and the confirmed edges as leaves. Together these trees have $V-2$ internal nodes and $V$ leaves, which gives $2+(V-2)+V=2V$ calls, including the initialization. For a segment, the two directed copies of the chord give four calls. \Cref{thm:main} bounds $V$, regardless of how many permutations represent a vertex.

title: Proof
body_md: \Cref{prop:es} gives exactly $2V$ oracle calls, for points and segments as well. Lexicographic assignment uses ordered pairs of costs and cubic componentwise arithmetic (\Cref{sec:polygon-reconstruction}). We apply this to the polygons of \Cref{lem:reduction} for $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ or $\mathrm O(2)$. By \Cref{thm:main}, the total is $\mathcal O(n^5)$ arithmetic operations; bit costs are separate. For input coordinates with rational real and imaginary parts, the oracle costs and the edge normals are rational, which permits exact verification of the returned polygon (\Cref{prop:optimality,app:verification}).

title: Proof
body_md:
Recomputing the correlations of the returned matchings gives a hull $\widehat{\mathcal P}\subseteq\mathcal P(a,b)$. Exact signs of $(z'-z)\times(w-z)$ determine its distinct extreme points and verify their reported order up to a cyclic shift. For each edge of a two-dimensional $\widehat{\mathcal P}$, we check that the assignment optimum in the outward normal direction equals the support value of the edge. The corresponding half-planes contain $\mathcal P(a,b)$ and intersect in $\widehat{\mathcal P}$, which proves the reverse inclusion.
The lower-dimensional cases require checks along the hull as well as across it. For a segment, the two opposite normal directions confine $\mathcal P(a,b)$ to its line, and the initial lexicographic queries bound its endpoints, through the secondary extrema if the line is vertical. If the initial points coincide, equality of the primary extrema gives a vertical line, and equality of the opposite secondary extrema gives a single point. Thus $\widehat{\mathcal P}=\mathcal P(a,b)$ in all cases, and convexity reduces the maximum to an exact comparison of the squared moduli of the vertices.

title: Proof
body_md: For an arc of half-width $h_\theta\le\pi/3$, let $v$ be a vertex with the smallest queried value and let $M$ attain it. The minimum $L_I$ of the interpolant over the arc is at least $F(v)$. If $v$ is an endpoint, its matching is already feasible there. Otherwise $v=\sec(h_\theta)u_0$, where $u_0$ is the midpoint of the arc on the circle, and $g_M(u_0)\le F(v)+\kappa_\theta(\sec h_\theta-1)$. Fitting the returned matchings therefore gives a feasible value $U_I$ with $U_I-L_I\le \kappa_\theta(\sec h_\theta-1)\le \kappa_\theta h_\theta^2$, since $\cos h_\theta\ge1/2$. For $\kappa_\theta>0$, the depth $d_{\rm tree}=\max\{0,\lceil\tfrac12\log_2(\kappa_\theta(\pi/3)^2/\varepsilon)\rceil\}$ suffices. A fully evaluated cell at that depth has $L_I\ge U-\varepsilon$ for the global incumbent cost $U$, so the best-bound search terminates before it subdivides the cell. The three binary trees up to depth $d_{\rm tree}$ contain $3(2^{d_{\rm tree}+1}-1)$ cells, each of which requires three queries. If $\kappa_\theta=0$, the objective is constant in the yaw and the initial evaluations suffice.

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) For an arc of half-width $h_\theta\le\pi/3$, the smallest of the three triangle values is attained at an endpoint or at the apex $\sec(h_\theta)u(\mu)$. Fitting the matching returned there over the arc gives a feasible value that exceeds the minimum of the interpolant by at most $\kappa_\theta(\sec h_\theta-1)\le \kappa_\theta h_\theta^2$, as in the proof of \Cref{prop:gravity-accuracy}; hence $F^*_A-L_A\le \kappa_\theta h_\theta^2$. If one matching $M$ attains all three values, then $F\le g_M=\ell$ on the triangle and $F\ge\ell$ by \Cref{lem:arc-interpolation}, so $L_A=\min_A g_M=F^*_A$.

(ii) We fix the translation at zero in both examples. For the radius bound, take one source point $x=(1,0,0)$ and one target $y=(2,0,0)$. Then $F(\theta)=5-4\cos\theta$, with minimum $1$ at $\theta=0$. On an arc centered at $\mu$, the radius bound is $(r_{\rm res}(\mu)-2\sin(h_\theta/2))_+^2$ with $r_{\rm res}(\mu)=(5-4\cos\mu)^{1/2}\ge1$. For the arc centered at the minimizer, $F^*_A=1$ and the gap is $1-(1-2\sin(h_\theta/2))^2=4\sin(h_\theta/2)-4\sin^2(h_\theta/2)\ge2\sin(h_\theta/2)\ge2h_\theta/\pi$, since $\sin(h_\theta/2)\le1/2$ for $h_\theta\le\pi/3$. For the independent-edge bound, take the sources $(\pm1,0,0)$ and the targets $(\pm\cos a,\sin a,0)$ with $\pi/3\le a<\pi/2$, matched by sign, so that $h_\theta\le a$ on every admissible arc. The two edges prefer the yaws $a$ and $-a$. The sign matching costs $4-4\cos a\cos\theta$ and the crossed matching $4+4\cos a\cos\theta$, so $F=4-4\cos a\,|\cos\theta|$ has its minimum $4-4\cos a$ at $\theta=0$. On $[-h_\theta,h_\theta]$, each edge is minimized at the endpoint nearer its preferred yaw and the crossed matching gives no less, so the bound is $4-4\cos(a-h_\theta)$ and the gap is $4(\cos(a-h_\theta)-\cos a)=8\sin(a-h_\theta/2)\sin(h_\theta/2)\ge(8/\pi)\sin(a/2)\,h_\theta$.

(iii) We now convert the local gap of the radius bound into a lower bound on the work of the search. Put $r=\sqrt\varepsilon$ and assume $0<\varepsilon\le1/40000$.
Since $r_{\rm res}(\mu)^2\le1+2\mu^2$, we have $r_{\rm res}(\mu)\le1+\mu^2$.
For $0\le h_\theta\le\pi/3$, the radius bound is below $1-\varepsilon$ whenever
$\mu^2<2h_\theta/\pi-\varepsilon$; this uses $\sin(h_\theta/2)\ge h_\theta/\pi$ and $\zeta^2\le\zeta$ on $[0,1]$.

For the counting argument, we retain both children of every split, including arcs that were pruned earlier. The three
roots, centered at $-2\pi/3$, $0$ and $2\pi/3$ with half-width $\pi/3$, cover
$[-\pi,\pi]$, and bisection preserves this cover. If a terminal certificate uses an
inherited bound, we contract its subtree at a certifying ancestor. The contracted
forest still covers the roots and has no more expansions. Each terminal leaf
now has a direct radius bound $L\ge1-\varepsilon$: the original feasible
incumbent satisfies $U\ge1$, even when it differs between leaves, and the zero
floor cannot certify this threshold. The central root cannot be terminal by
this criterion, so its descendants have $h_\theta\le\pi/6$.

A descendant that meets $[-r,r]$ satisfies $|\mu|\le h_\theta+r$. If $h_\theta\ge100\varepsilon$,
then $h_\theta>0$, $h_\theta<11/20$ and $r\le1/200$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:radius-terminal-width}
 \mu^2+\varepsilon\le\tfrac{57}{100}h_\theta+2\varepsilon
 \le\tfrac{59}{100}h_\theta<\tfrac35h_\theta<\tfrac{2h_\theta}{\pi},
\end{equation}
using $\pi<3.15$. Such an arc cannot be terminal. Thus each terminal leaf
covers at most $200\varepsilon$ of $[-r,r]$. Covered lengths add under bisection,
so the central tree has $N_{\rm leaf}\ge1/(100r)$ leaves and $N_{\rm leaf}-1\ge1/(200r)$ expanded
nodes, since $r\le1/200$. This proves the lower bound independently of
the order in which best-first search breaks ties.

With the Rubix bound, the objective for the single correspondence,
$\|\widehat R(u)x-y\|^2+(1-\|u\|^2)\|x_{xy}\|^2$, is affine in $u$, so by~(i)
each root bound equals the minimum over its arc. Fitting the returned matching gives
$U=1$ at $\theta=0$. The central root has bound $1$, and the other two have
bounds $5-4\cos(\pi/3)=3$, so the search stops after the root evaluations.
The separation concerns the displayed bounds: adding the global norm bound
$(\|y\|-\|x\|)^2=1$ also solves this particular radius-bound example immediately.
